blocks.text: Draft for Jared's approval. Every rule in the table was read on the city's or the Province's own page on 2026-11-01. Where a page did not state a number or a date, the cell says so. The Township of Langley and White Rock are still to be added.

Multiplex potential means a lot where you could build more than one house, and it is one of the most common reasons buyers pay a premium for an ordinary-looking house. It is real in many places and false in others, and the difference comes down to a few rules that you can check before you make an offer.

Under the Province's small-scale multi-unit housing rules, municipalities must allow at least three units on single-family and duplex lots of 280 m² or smaller, and at least four on lots larger than 280 m². On lots larger than 280 m² near frequent bus service, they must allow six. A bus stop counts as frequent if at least one route stops there at least every 15 minutes on average from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays, or 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekends.

The rules apply to areas inside an urban containment boundary and to municipalities with more than 5,000 people, with some exemptions. Under Bill 25 (2025), local governments were to update their bylaws by June 30, 2026 unless they had an extension. Secondary suites and accessory dwelling units are allowed in single-family zones across the province where the three-to-six-unit rules do not apply.
Cities wrote their own bylaws to meet the Province's minimums, so numbers, dates and conditions differ. This table gathers what each city's own pages say.

blocks.text: Checks before you pay for multiplex potential
The unit count in a listing is a claim, not a permit. Before you rely on it, check the following, most of which come straight from the city rules above.

First, the zone. Eligibility starts with single-family or duplex zoning, so a lot in a comprehensive development zone follows its own bylaw. Surrey's page, for example, sets separate extra-unit rules by lot size for its CD zones.

Second, the lot area. The thresholds sit at 280 m² or 281 m² and, in Pitt Meadows and Maple Ridge, at 4,050 m² (about one acre). A lot a few square metres short of a threshold changes the answer, so get the survey figure and not the listing figure.

Third, the distance to frequent transit. Six units depend on being within 400 m of a qualifying bus stop, and the cities publish tools or maps for this. Fourth, services and exclusions: Pitt Meadows excludes heritage properties and lots not connected to water or sewer, and Maple Ridge does not allow secondary suites in its floodplain area.

Last, the cost of getting there. Maple Ridge requires an Engineering Service Review before a building permit, and Surrey says a building permit is needed for any multi-unit build. Surrey also says units built without permits are not made legal after the fact, so ask for the permit record.

A suite is the simplest way to add income. Maple Ridge permits one secondary suite per lot, inside the same building as a single detached house, no larger than 40% of the building's gross floor area and not in the floodplain area. Surrey's page says a house may have only one secondary suite under the BC Building Code, and that the City does not make unpermitted suites or coach houses legal retroactively. White Rock lists a registered secondary suite and an accessory dwelling unit as separate accessory uses and allows only one of its listed accessory uses at a time.

faq.a: Not automatically. The Province sets four units as the minimum a city must allow on single-family and duplex lots over 280 m², with some exemptions, and each city then applies it to its own zones. Surrey, Pitt Meadows, Maple Ridge, Delta and Chilliwack publish this 280 m² threshold. Langley City's bylaw allows up to four units in its RS1 and RS2 zones without stating a lot-size threshold. Check the lot's zone, its surveyed area and any exclusions.
faq.q: Does a lot over 280 m² automatically allow four units?

faq.a: Being within 400 m of a frequent bus stop, meaning a route that stops at least every 15 minutes on average during the Province's set weekday and weekend hours, on a lot the city's rules allow it for. The Province's tier is for lots larger than 280 m². Surrey, Pitt Meadows, Maple Ridge, Delta and Langley City all describe a six-unit tier near frequent bus service.

The Province prohibits public hearings for the zoning amendments that implement the rules, and Maple Ridge says most developments under them do not need public notice. A building permit is still required.
faq.q: Do I need a public hearing or neighbour approval to build under these rules?
